extracted.intended_audience: general Wikipedia readers; fans and researchers of television and comedy
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and descriptive criteria for creating/evaluating a surreal, prank-oriented late-night talk/sketch show in the style of The Eric Andre Show. Covers tone, format, production constraints, interview tactics, and season-level aesthetic choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre blend: parody, surrealism, black comedy, sketch/prank elements
rubrics_metrics.description: The series is described as 'A parody of late night talk shows' and as containing surreal humor, black comedy, sketch comedy and prank show elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Episodes mix monologues incorporating black comedy and surrealism, surreal celebrity interviews, short sketches, candid camera footage, and non sequiturs. A successful show in this vein intentionally blends parody of the talk-show form with absurd and prank-based components to create its comedic identity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinct episode structure and opening stunt
rubrics_metrics.description: Each episode opens on the show's main set... André runs onto set and destroys the backdrop, desk, and various furnishings around him. Once the song is completed, stagehands swiftly remove the broken furniture and replace it with identical pieces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The opening destructive stunt establishes tone and rhythm: a violent/chaotic entrance, rapid reset, then the co-host arrival and monologue. Repeating and ritualizing a disruptive opening is a formal device to set audience and guest expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Host persona: exaggerated, aggressive, and discomforting
rubrics_metrics.description: Both host Eric André and co-host Hannibal Buress play exaggerated caricatures of themselves, with André being consistently eccentric, dysfunctional, violent and psychotic, while Buress serves as a relative straight man.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The host should overact, act aggressively toward crew, divert from script, and actively attempt to make guests uncomfortable as a performance tactic. The co-host functions as a foil/straight man who highlights the host's absurdity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interview tactics: surprise, exhaustion, and 'first moment / exhausted end' editing
rubrics_metrics.description: Co-director Andrew Barchilon: 'We almost always use the first moment of an interview... And then we skip to the end, when they're exhausted and confused. That's where the gold is.' Co-director Kitao Sakurai described season 3's interview methods as 'Vietcong interrogation tactics.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use surprise, abruptness and sequences that wear down or disorient guests to elicit unrehearsed reactions. Tactics include capturing initial stunned responses, engineering physical discomfort (e.g., rotten clams, heat ducts), and selective editing to juxtapose early and late moments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Season-level stylistic cohesion and variation
rubrics_metrics.description: André has expressed that each season of the show is shot with a unique style in mind, intended to be thematically cohesive while remaining distinct from other seasons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan a coherent visual and thematic approach per season (camera type, set dressing, costumes, hair/makeup, lighting). Examples: Season 1 vintage Ikegami cameras and dark set; Season 3 tropical plants and upbeat vibe; Season 4 a dark 'Eraserhead' dystopian tone; Season 5 vibrant decorations and green screen.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editing approach: heavily edited vs live-to-tape
rubrics_metrics.description: André commented that filming live-to-tape is 'kind of difficult' and: 'I think you can fit in more jokes per square inch in something that's heavily edited.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer heavy editing to compress, refine and escalate comedic beats; live-to-tape may capture rawness but can limit density of jokes. Choose format according to whether the priority is polished rapid-fire humor or raw live chaos.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards & Production / broadcast constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: The Eric Andre Show received notes from 'Standards and Production' at Adult Swim, particularly regarding suicide, drug use and insulting specific deities: André commented that 'I can curse out God, but I can't curse out Jesus'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When planning provocative material, account for network/legal/content standards. Expect specific restrictions (e.g., depictions or insults regarding certain religious figures, graphic depictions of self-harm or drug use) and prepare alternative staging or framing to satisfy standards notes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consent, jurisdictional consent laws and permitting
rubrics_metrics.description: Because of the difficulties with gaining consent under California's regulations, some of the impromptu and hidden camera sketches had to be re-recorded in New York City. Man-on-the-street filming encountered permit and safety issues (e.g., police response for dragging a body bag; $300 filming permits; Hazmat warnings for sewer stunts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for local consent laws and permitting requirements when planning hidden-camera or public stunts; be prepared to relocate shoots or re-record segments to comply. Factor the cost and logistics of permits and the legal risk of arrests into production planning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guest briefing strategy and ethics
rubrics_metrics.description: André stated they 'would very reluctantly or not at all tell the celebrity guests the name of the show so that they'd just come in blind.' The show also used impersonators and fake guests in earlier seasons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliberately limiting guest briefing can produce more authentic reactions but raises ethical and legal issues; weigh the comedic value of surprise against informed-consent norms and potential guest harm or fallout.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of shock, gross-out and provocative stunts
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples include André eating his own vomit (actually oatmeal) to make a guest flee, splashing subway riders with cereal and milk, dragging a leaking body bag through Chinatown, and other gross or violent spectacles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shock/gross-out elements can produce strong and memorable comedic reactions, but they carry safety, ethical, and permitting consequences and may damage relationships with guests or communities. Plan for cleanup, legal risk, and reputation management.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recurring performance elements and parody of amateur acts
rubrics_metrics.description: At the end, a performer of some type plays over the ending credits; ending performances are usually parodies of amateur acts common to public-access television; the house band regularly participates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a predictable but variable closing element (parodied amateur acts, house band bits) to reinforce show identity and provide a counterpoint to interview segments. Recurring troupe elements build continuity and audience expectation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writer and production team structure
rubrics_metrics.description: The core writing cast consists of André, the show's directorial team Andrew Barchilon and Kitao Sakurai, as well as other named writers and an editor who joined beginning season two.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Embed writing within the directing/producing team and include an editor in the creative staff. Maintain a small core writers' room supplemented by recurring contributors to preserve a consistent voice while allowing new material and performers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetic influences and intentional framing as 'deconstruction'
rubrics_metrics.description: The show was partly influenced by Space Ghost Coast to Coast, Chris Farley, Tom Green, Da Ali G Show, Conan O'Brien, and others. Co-director Kitao Sakurai called it more of a 'deconstruction, an alternate reality talk show' rather than a spoof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ground the show's approach in avant-garde/anti-talk-show precedents and consciously position it as deconstructive: rather than merely mimicking, alter the talk-show grammar to expose or subvert conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize authentic confusion/discomfort over polished comfort
rubrics_metrics.description: Critical reception notes that the show 'thrives on the genuine confusion and discomfort of its guests' and functions as a deconstruction of the genre by stripping away the safety and predictability of typical promotional interviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure comedic success by the authenticity of guest reactions and audience perception of unpredictability. Designing bits to produce real bewilderment can be more valuable than tightly staged, entirely safe sketches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan for performer safety and medical readiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Filming produced numerous injuries: André suffered injuries during production, a concussion when hit in the head during a set-destruction intro, stitches from a window stunt, and other medical incidents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While physical risk may be part of the aesthetic, include thorough stunt planning, safety protocols, and on-set medical readiness. Track and mitigate risks where possible; document acceptable vs unacceptable levels of performer injury.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deliberate production and design choices to influence guest reaction
rubrics_metrics.description: Production choices such as not running the studio air conditioning (because it was too loud) had the added effect of making guests feel uncomfortable. Visual/technical choices (camera type, lighting) were used to shape season tone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use environmental and technical production decisions (sound, temperature, camera format, lighting, set dressing) intentionally to influence guest comfort and audience perception. These choices can be tools for both mood and comedic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editing ethics and potential misrepresentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Instances are cited where guests complained about possibly misleading editing (e.g., Flavor Flav disputed a freeze-frame implying he was kicked; he claimed the kick 'NEVER HAPPENED' and blamed editing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editing can heighten comedy but also create disputed portrayals of guests; weigh the comedic benefit against ethical considerations and possible reputational/relational harm. Maintain documentation of raw footage when possible to address disputes.
